title: Roofs Around the World
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Houses are shaped by the places in which they are built. Walk through any town in the world, and you will notice how the roofs differ: some are flat, others steeply sloped, and some rise into domes or tall points. Architects and builders did not choose these shapes only for their appearance. Most roof types were developed over centuries to deal with local weather, to use the materials that were available, and to meet the needs of those who lived beneath them. In this passage, five basic types are described, from the simple flat roof to the tall spire, and the effects of modern materials and of the changing climate are considered at the end.

In hot, dry regions, such as the deserts of the Middle East and North Africa, houses usually have flat roofs. There is little rain, so the water does not need to run off, and a flat roof is simple to build from mud brick and wooden beams. It also serves as an extra room. In summer, families sleep on it to escape the heat of the night, and in the daytime it is used for drying fruit, washing and storing grain.

In places where there is heavy rain or snow, the roof is usually pitched, which means that it slopes steeply from a central ridge down to the walls on each side. Rain runs off quickly, and snow slides to the ground instead of piling up and breaking the roof. In the mountains of Switzerland and Norway, roofs may be inclined at an angle of forty-five degrees or more, and many have a wide overhang to protect the walls from melting snow.

A dome is a different solution, and it is found mainly on large public buildings. The Romans perfected the technique, and their Pantheon, built about 1,900 years ago, has a dome that remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Domes were later used for mosques, such as those in Samarkand and Istanbul, and for churches and observatories. Because a dome has no corners, it distributes its weight evenly, and it can cover a large space without internal columns.

The spire is tall and thin, narrowing to a point. It is common on churches in Europe, where it rises above the town as a landmark and, in the Middle Ages, as a sign of the builders' devotion. The tallest spires, such as that of Ulm Minster in Germany at 161 metres, took generations to complete. Because they are exposed to wind and lightning, they are fitted with iron frames and conductors, and every few decades they require expensive repairs. Many have needed major repairs, and some have been rebuilt completely after fires or wars.

Modern materials have changed the pattern. With steel and reinforced concrete, builders can cover wide areas with flat roofs even in rainy countries, using waterproof membranes to keep the water out. Roofs may also be planted with grass and flowers, which cool the building in summer and reduce flooding in cities by absorbing rainwater. Dr Elif Demir, an architect, believes that the roof, long neglected as a mere cover, may become one of the most useful parts of the city building.

Climate change is likely to alter roof design once again. In countries where the summers are becoming hotter, designers are rediscovering white and reflective surfaces, which bounce back the sunlight, and shaded terraces. In regions that are expected to receive more heavy rain, drainage is being redesigned. Roofs are also being fitted with solar panels in large numbers, and some countries now require them on new houses. The oldest part of the building is thus becoming the newest.
